title: Acceptance and rising spirits
hookLine: bhaana and chardi kala belong together

cards: Bow your head, or lift it? Some people hear acceptance and think of giving up. Some hear rising spirits and think of fighting fate.
Two words have walked through this stretch of the path: bhaana, the will, the sweet acceptance of what the Lord sends, and chardi kala, rising spirits. Side by side, they can look like opposites.
One bows; the other lifts. The Sikh tradition doesn't choose between them. It says them in a single breath, at the very end of the Ardas.

teach.b: First, the line. Yesterday's words again: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits, and then, by your will, the good of all.
Rising and accepting share one sentence, and neither cancels the other. Second, a refrain.
In the Japji, Guru Nanak stops at the end of a pauri, overwhelmed by the size of creation, and says, in paraphrase: whatever pleases you, that alone is good; you are forever whole, formless One.
Jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar. The next pauri ends with the same words, and the next.
Acceptance there isn't one grim moment; it's a line the Japji keeps coming back to. Third, what acceptance isn't. Bhaana doesn't mean liking injustice or sitting still.
The same people who recite that refrain every morning run free kitchens and stand up to wrong. Acceptance is about the ground under your feet: this happened. Rising is about the next step: and now.
Fourth, the hinge. Accept first, so your strength stops pouring into fighting what already is. Then rise, so it can pour into what can still be done.
A farmer wakes to find hail has flattened the field. Bhaana says: it happened, and it's in the Lord's hands. Chardi kala says: there's seed in the shed.

how: Sikhs speak of living in bhaana, God's will, while keeping chardi kala, rising spirits; the two are joined in the closing words of the Ardas, and the Japji's refrain 'jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar' voices the acceptance.

games.q: what does “acceptance and rising spirits” mean?
o: accepting what has come, then rising to act
fighting hard against whatever life sends
giving up quietly on what you can't change

games.q: accept, then rise: tap the pairs.
p: jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar

s: accepting the will means giving up
bhaana settles the ground; chardi kala takes the next step. accept, then rise.
bhaana and chardi kala are joined in one line of the Ardas
nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala.
in the Japji, the line on what pleases the One comes back as a refrain
jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar closes one pauri, then the next, and the next.

games.q: hail flattens your crop the week before harvest. what does accept, then rise look like?
o: curse the sky until next season.
say it's fine and pretend it didn't happen.
games.why: bhaana says it happened; chardi kala says there's seed in the shed. the two belong together.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you can't change today, a loss, a diagnosis, a decision someone else made, and on the breaths out, let it simply be true: this happened.

On the breaths in, ask one quiet question, and now?, and let one small next step show itself: a call, a meal, a walk, some rest. If you pray, hold the Japji's words in mind: jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar.
If a loss ever feels like more than you can hold, reach out: 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Acceptance and rising spirits. Bhaana and chardi kala, said in one line of the Ardas: accept what has come, then rise toward what can be done. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the will, what pleases the Lord; tere bhaane means by your will.

carryVoice: Your line: accept, then rise. Two halves of one breath, said together. Rest well.
